messages.subject_clean: Issues with R Studio?
messages.body_plain:
Hello all!

Is anyone else having issues installing packages (specifically ggmap, OpenStreetMap, rJava and rgdal) in R Studio?

Every time I try to load library(OpenStreetMap), I get this:

ERROR: configuration failed for package ‘rgdal’
* removing ‘/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/3.4/Resources/library/rgdal’
Warning in install.packages :
  installation of package ‘rgdal’ had non-zero exit status

OR

Error: package or namespace load failed for ‘OpenStreetMap’:
 .onLoad failed in loadNamespace() for 'rJava', details:
  call: dyn.load(file, DLLpath = DLLpath, ...)
  error: unable to load shared object '/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/3.4/Resources/library/rJava/libs/rJava.so':
  dlopen(/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/3.4/Resources/library/rJava/libs/rJava.so, 6): Library not loaded: @rpath/libjvm.dylib
  Referenced from: /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/3.4/Resources/library/rJava/libs/rJava.so
  Reason: image not found

I realized that a lot of the issues I’m having in my analysis are coming from the fact that these packages are no longer working with my R Studio, although they used to work based on my former code…Do I need to install a different version of R?

Alex

Alexandra McInturf

Biotelemetry Laboratory
University of California, Davis

GET(url, config = list(sign_oauth2.0 = key)) # Status 401

Simon said that the newest binary uses a much newer version of java.
"Apple has dropped Java support many years ago - what you have a is a left-over from a very old OS X version as you likely upgraded your OS X over the years without re-installing.
Since R 3.4.0 the CRAN binary uses Java 1.8, because too many users have complained about incompatibilities with old Java version, so you have two options
1) recompile rJava from sources against your ancient Java
2) install Java 1.8 from Oracle[1], then run R CMD javareconf"

Running Linux from a USB, depending on the installation type consumes
quite a bit of RAM. You don't have much to begin with, so that
experience might not be great. It's quite easy to make a Live Linux usb
and test. As long as you read/write data from your main computer drive
the RAM should be the only big limitation. If you set up a persistent
usb stick which allows software upgrades within linux and saving files
to the stick that will perform even slower. VirtualBox may or may not be
any better considering how much ram you have, but is probably better. It
is by far easier than other options because you can easily redo, or try
different things. Picking a less graphics intensive distro would help,
or if you really want to jump in install a server variant and get no GUI.

I tested Windows Linux subshell installation the other day, following
instructions like
https://answers.microsoft.com/en-us/insider/wiki/insider_wintp-insider_install/how-to-enable-the-windows-subsystem-for-linux/16e8f2e8-4a6a-4325-a89a-fd28c7841775
Talk to your dept IT if you need help.

Considering your hardware I would recommend the following:
1. Get access to a computer cluster on campus, chances are your dept or
advisor belongs to at least once group who has access to one.
2. Use a cloud service, you can get 12 months free use of Amazon AWS
micro instance. Paying for something more to test HDFS etc for a few
minutes/hours at a time won't break the bank. There's even
pre-configured Hadoop deployments.
3. Upgrade the RAM in your laptop, it's probably capable of 8-16 GB of
RAM for $100 or less.

Cygwin is not worth it. I would dual boot before that. Of the local
options dual booting would perform the best but is also the trickiest to
setup (though not usually hard, backup 1st).

If you have more questions, consider the email lists on http://lugod.org
the local linux user group and the #linux channel on
https://ucdavis.slack.com

Enjoy,

crd <- as.data.frame(coordinates(res))

messages.body_plain:
It is always good to learn some debugging tools when you start writing functions - Duncan Temple Lang with the DSI has put up some pretty good resources.

In this cause, you are running into issues with scoping. You are calculating a value inside of a for-loop, but not recording it anywhere. This works as intended:

wc_calc <- function (diameter) {
    ans = numeric(length(time_data)-1)

    for (i in 1 : (length (time_data) - 1)) {
            a <- theta [(time_data [i] + 1) : (time_data [i+1] - 1),]
            aa <- na.omit (as.vector (as.matrix (t (a))))

            ans[i] = mean (as.double (aa [diameter]))
    }
    return(ans)
}

That said, there are much better ways to do this calculation - the function above relies on Global variables (things in your environment), which can be a huge source of bugs. Additionally, for loops are very slow in R, and we tend to try to write vectorized code when possible.

Have you verified that the code above is actually working correctly? I am a bit confused by what you are referring to as "nodes" and "coordinates", etc., but I have a feeling that these lines are not doing what you think they are:

 aa <- na.omit (as.vector (as.matrix (t (a))))

 wc$diameter [i] <- mean (as.double (aa [diameter]))

In particular, how do you know that "diameter" is indexing correctly into your data that has been transposed, collapsed into a vector column-wise, and then cleaned of NAs? If there are any NA values, the correct index into "aa" will shift, so you will pull out different values depending on whether or not there are NAs.  I would check that you are getting the correct answer before worrying about making it more efficient.

Assuming your "node" is the position row-wise of the value you want according to:

1 2 3 4
5 6 7 8
...

then the "node" x resides in column:

x%%n_column#(where 0 means in column n_column

and in row:

ceiling(x/n_column)

Therefore, you can get your indices of interest with:

rows = ceiling(dia10/ncol(theta))
cols = dia10 %% ncol(theta)
cols[cols == 0] = ncol(theta)

of_interest = cbind(rows, cols)

Now, you just subset your matrix by this. Other tricks: your time_data are evenly spaced (unique(diff(time_data))), so you can just calculate how far you need to jump from each starting point.

To put it (mostly) altogether: (Disclaimer - I am pretty sure this works, but I did not test it thoroughly. Make sure you verify before using.)

# using dia10
rows = ceiling(dia10/ncol(theta))
cols = dia10 %% ncol(theta)
cols[cols == 0] = ncol(theta)

of_interest = cbind(rows, cols)

start = time_data + 1
jump = unique(diff(time_data)) - 1

foo = function(start, jump, theta, of_interest)
{
    sapply(seq_along(start), function(i, start, jump, theta, of_interest){
        a = theta[start[i]:(start[i] + jump),]
        tmp = as.numeric(as.matrix(a)[of_interest])
        mean(tmp, na.rm = TRUE)
    }, start, jump, theta, of_interest)
}

You should also wrap the part to convert from the "node" to row,col in a function.
